summary: Help 5-6 year olds move from naming shapes by their overall look to describing them by countable parts: sides and corners for flat (2-D) shapes; flat faces, edges and corners for solids (3-D). The central work is attending to component attributes rather than the holistic silhouette, comparing two shapes on a single countable property, and grasping that each flat face of a solid is itself a 2-D shape. Best taught with real, handleable shapes children touch and count, with varied examples so attention shifts from appearance to structure. Corner/face counting is clearest with flat-faced solids such as cubes and cuboids; curved solids (sphere, cylinder, cone) are described by their curved surfaces. On-screen rotatable models may add value by exposing hidden back features and peeling faces, but complement rather than replace physical handling.
misconceptions: Judges a shape by its overall look or size rather than counting its sides/corners (the bigger-drawn shape 'has more').
Counts only the sides/corners/faces that are visible in a picture or facing them, missing the hidden ones.
Uses everyday words loosely — 'corner' and 'side' blur the difference between a solid's face, edge and vertex.
Treats a 3-D solid as if it were the 2-D shape of one of its faces (calls a cube 'a square').

activities.title: Count by touching and marking every part
steps: Hold a physical 2-D tile to count its sides and corners, or a flat-faced solid such as a cube or cuboid to count its corners and flat faces (curved solids like a sphere, cylinder or cone have curved surfaces rather than a full set of flat faces and corners, so describe those separately).
Count each side, corner or flat face by touching it and placing a sticker or pen mark on each one as it is counted, so none is double-counted or missed.
For a flat-faced solid (cube, cuboid), turn it over and count again from a different starting face to check the total stays the same.
activities.insight: A shape's number of sides/corners/flat faces is found by systematically counting all of them, including the ones round the back, not by guessing from the front view.

activities.title: Compare two shapes on one countable property
steps: Look at a triangle drawn large and a rectangle drawn small, placed side by side.
Decide which has more sides, and count each side by touching and marking it.
Say which has more sides and how you know, using the count rather than the size.
activities.insight: Which shape has more sides is decided by counting, not by which is drawn bigger: the count is independent of size and orientation.

activities.title: Each face is a 2-D shape; flat vs solid
steps: Point to one face of a cube and name its 2-D shape ('this face is a square').
Check whether all the faces are the same 2-D shape.

Compare a single thin tile with the whole cube: the tile is almost flat and shows one 2-D shape, while the cube has depth and six flat faces. Note that a real tile or card has a little thickness but stands for an ideal flat shape, so talk about the shape it represents rather than whether you can pick it up.
Match everyday objects to solids and, where they have them, their flat faces (ball = sphere, no flat faces; box = cuboid, rectangle faces; can = cylinder, two circle faces and a curved surface).
activities.insight: A flat-faced solid such as a cube has flat faces that are 2-D shapes, but the solid is not the same as one of those faces: a cube is not 'a square'. Curved solids such as a sphere have curved surfaces instead of, or as well as, flat faces.

activities.title: Predict then count a cube's corners
steps: Before counting, predict out loud how many corners the cube has altogether and say the number.
Turn and mark every corner together, counting the ones round the back.
Compare the predicted number with the counted total of 8, and talk about the corners that were hidden.
activities.insight: Looking at the front of a solid under-counts its parts; turning it reveals hidden corners, so a solid has features all the way round.

activities.title: Explore hidden structure with a rotatable solid model (optional complement)
steps: On screen, spin a solid-coloured (non-see-through) cube and tap each corner you can see; each tagged corner keeps a glowing dot that stays, so none is double-counted.
Keep turning the cube until the untagged corners from the back swing into view, and tag those too.
Tap a face so it peels off as a flat square that floats into a '2-D shapes' tray, separating the flat square from the solid block.
Alongside the screen, handle real wooden solids and count their corners and faces by touch.
activities.insight: A solid has features all the way round, and each flat face is a 2-D shape that can be seen apart from the solid; a model that persists tags and peels faces makes both ideas concrete.

activities.title: Break the prototype with wonky and atypical shapes
steps: Examine long thin triangles, tilted rectangles, and squares with a non-horizontal base.

Count the sides and corners of each; for squares and rectangles also check that the corners are square corners (and, for a square, that all sides are the same length); then decide whether it is still the named shape.

Sort examples from non-examples, explaining the decision by the shape's sides and corners (how many, and for squares and rectangles whether the corners are square and the sides equal) rather than by how typical the shape looks.
activities.insight: A shape is defined by its properties (number and kind of sides/corners), not by matching a single typical picture or a particular orientation.

checkQuestion: Put a real cube in the child's hands. Ask: 'What shape are the flat faces of this cube, and how many corners does it have? Tell me how you worked out the number of corners.'
checkAnswer: The faces are squares; the cube has 8 corners (vertices). Crucially, the child counts systematically — turning the cube or accounting for the corners they cannot see — rather than counting only the ones facing them. Informal 'corners' for vertices is fine at this age.
